items.title: [@bytebase/dbhub] DBHub: MySQL and MariaDB comment interpretation bypasses read-only SQL validation
items.summary: The read-only mode can be bypassed on the MySQL and MariaDB connectors. In read-only mode a caller can still execute arbitrary write and DDL statements (for example DROP TABLE), which defeats the protection that read-only mode is meant to provide when a database is exposed to an AI agent.Root causeThe problem is a mismatch between how DBHub's SQL parser handles single-line comments and how MySQL and MariaDB actually parse them.In src/utils/sql-parser.ts, scanSingleLineComment treats "--" as the start of a comment no matter what character follows it. MySQL and MariaDB only begin a "--" comment when the two dashes are followed by whitespace, a control character, or the end of the line. Otherwise the dashes are read as two minus signs and the rest of the line is ordinary SQL.The read-only check in src/tools/execute-sql.ts splits the input and validates each statement with isReadOnlySQL, but the connector then executes the original, unmodified string. The MySQL and MariaDB connectors open their connection pool with multipleStatements: true (src/connectors/mysql/index.ts:54 and src/connectors/mariadb/index.ts:53) and run the whole string in a single call.Because of this, the following payload:SELECT 1--1;DROP TABLE victimis seen by DBHub as a single SELECT statement, since everything after "--" is treated as a comment and the read-only check passes. MySQL and MariaDB instead parse it as "SELECT 1 - -1" followed by "DROP TABLE victim" and execute both statements.Proof of conceptDBHub's own parser. Running splitSQLStatements and isReadOnlySQL from this repository on the payload returns a single statement and readOnly = true, so the query is allowed in read-only mode. The same code correctly rejects "SELECT 1; DROP TABLE victim", which confirms that the "--1" is what gets through.Execution. Connecting to MariaDB 11.4 with mysql2 and multipleStatements: true (the same option the connector uses) and sending the payload returns 2 for the first statement, which confirms "--" was not treated as a comment, and then drops the table. The table exists before the call and is gone afterwards.ImpactRead-only mode is the control operators rely on to let an assistant read from a database without being able to change it. With this bypass, anyone who can influence the SQL the assistant sends, most realistically through prompt injection in content the assistant reads, can perform writes and destructive DDL against MySQL and MariaDB. PostgreSQL is not affected by this path, because it treats "--" as a comment regardless and executes each split statement individually.Affected code (current main, commit e99c3aa9, package version 0.22.3)src/utils/sql-parser.ts — scanSingleLineComment does not require whitespace after "--"src/tools/execute-sql.ts — validates the split statements but executes the original stringsrc/connectors/mysql/index.ts and src/connectors/mariadb/index.ts — multipleStatements: trueSuggested fixThe most reliable fix is to stop executing the original string: run only the statements that were validated, and disable multipleStatements on the MySQL and MariaDB connections unless it is genuinely required. As defense in depth, make the comment scanner dialect-aware so that for MySQL and MariaDB "--" only starts a comment when it is followed by whitespace, a control character, or the end of the line, similar to the handling already in place for MySQL conditional comments.Referenceshttps://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/security/advisories/GHSA-j656-3hf2-fvjchttps://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/pull/342https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/commit/872bb338f7d31f6afe517a076ac3e3edafaaaf08https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/releases/tag/v0.22.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j656-3hf2-fvjc

items.title: [@sd-jwt/decode] SD JWT JS: Tampered disclosures silently dropped instead of rejected
items.summary: SummaryWhen one Disclosure in an SD-JWT presentation is tampered so its digest no longer matches the Issuer-signed _sd array, @sd-jwt/decode 0.19.0 does not reject the presentation. It silently drops the unmatched Disclosure and returns a reduced claim set, reporting success. The Issuer signature is untouched and valid.This is a downgrade/omission primitive. A malicious or curious holder can present a tampered Disclosure and have the relying party receive fewer claims than the credential carries, with no error surfaced. Where the relying party does not enforce key binding, an in-transit (on-path) attacker can achieve the same by mangling one Disclosure's bytes; where key binding is enforced, on-path tampering instead breaks the holder's KB-JWT sd_hash binding (so it is rejected), and the downgrade is then exercisable by the key-bound holder — confirmed end-to-end with KB required.Two distinct tampering inputs converge on the same silent-drop sink:Genuinely non-decodable Disclosure (broken base64url -> bytes that are not valid UTF-8, e.g. an injected 0xF2 lead byte). RFC 9901 §7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1 require rejection. @sd-jwt/decode instead lossy-decodes it: the TextDecoder/Buffer path substitutes U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER) for the invalid byte and recovers a syntactically valid disclosure (the salt gains a U+FFFD, claim family_name = "Smith"). The recovered Disclosure then hashes to a digest absent from the signed _sd array, so it is silently skipped.Tampered-but-still-valid-JSON Disclosure (digest no longer matches _sd): same end state — the unmatched Disclosure is silently skipped.Two RFC 9901 MUSTs compound:§7.1 step 5 (primary): "If any Disclosure was not referenced by digest value in the Issuer-signed JWT (directly or recursively via other Disclosures), the SD-JWT MUST be rejected." — instead silently dropped.§7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1 (secondary): a non-base64url-JSON Disclosure MUST be rejected — the lenient lossy decode skips this check.Confirmed end-to-end through SDJwtInstance.verify() with a real ES256 issuer key, and again with key binding REQUIRED (a valid holder ES256 KB-JWT over aud+nonce+sd_hash).ImpactSilent claim-set reduction is a downgrade/omission primitive. If a relying party's authorization logic is "default-allow when a constraining claim is absent" (an age / role / restriction attribute), dropping that one Disclosure flips the decision, with no error surfaced. The decoder reporting success on a tampered presentation is the core problem; tampering should be a hard reject. Because SD-JWT VC and the EU EUDIW ARF profiles reuse this disclosure layer, the exposure is to wallet/verifier deployments built on @sd-jwt/*.Proof of concept (minimized — NOT a weaponized exploit)A clean single-mutation credential: lowercase _sd_alg: "sha-256", an honest Issuer body whose _sd digests are computed over the valid wire Disclosures, and exactly one wire byte-segment tampered — the family_name Disclosure made genuinely non-decodable (an invalid-UTF-8 0xF2 byte injected into its base64url). Everything else is byte-for-byte valid.The byte-exact credential cannot be faithfully pasted as text (it deliberately contains the invalid 0xF2 byte that triggers the lossy decode). It is provided as bug3_clean_tampered.cred with an untampered twin bug3_clean_control.cred, plus the minting script mint_bug3_clean.py and a three-oracle harness run_three_oracles.py — shared privately with the maintainer on first reply. Structure: 5 Disclosures, only index 1 (family_name) tampered; all other segments byte-for-byte valid.Observed on the byte-identical credential (three independent oracles):OracleVersionVerdictDetailRFC 9901 reference (pure Python)reference implREJECTR_DISCLOSURE_DECODEsd-jwt (Daniel Fett's reference impl)pip 0.10.4REJECTUnicodeDecodeError: 0xf2 ... invalid continuation byte@sd-jwt/decode (this package)0.19.0ACCEPTreduced set {given_name, email, vct, iss} — family_name silently dropped, no errorControl (untampered, same body): all three oracles ACCEPT the full 5-claim set including family_name: "Smith" — confirming the single tampered byte is the only difference. Liveness: the @sd-jwt/decode harness REJECTs pure garbage ("not-a-jwt", "~~~~", "aaa.bbb.ccc~ZZZZ~", "") and ACCEPTs the clean control, so the ACCEPT above is a genuine behavioral divergence, not an accept-everything stub. No ready-to-run exploit against any deployed verifier is included.Suggested fixIn the disclosure-decode loop of @sd-jwt/decode:Enforce §7.1 step 5: if any provided Disclosure is not referenced by a digest in the signed _sd array (directly or recursively), reject the entire presentation — do not silently skip it.Enforce §7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1: treat a Disclosure that fails base64url/JSON decode, or that is not a 3-element [salt, claimName, claimValue] array, as a fatal error. Replace the lenient TextDecoder/Buffer decode with a strict UTF-8 decode that throws on invalid bytes (do not substitute U+FFFD).Surface both rejections from the p
